title: Covalent Bonding
content:
# Covalent Bonding

## Learning Objectives

By the end of this lesson, you should be able to:
- Describe how covalent bonds form
- Explain why non-metals form covalent bonds
- Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for covalent molecules
- Distinguish between single, double, and triple bonds

## Introduction

**Covalent bonding** occurs when non-metal atoms share pairs of electrons. Unlike ionic bonding where electrons are transferred, covalent bonding involves atoms sharing electrons so that both achieve full outer shells.

## Key Concepts

### What is a Covalent Bond?

A **covalent bond** is a shared pair of electrons between two atoms.

When atoms share electrons:
- The shared electrons are attracted to the nuclei of BOTH atoms
- This attraction holds the atoms together
- Both atoms achieve a full outer shell

### Why Do Non-Metals Share Electrons?

Non-metals have many electrons in their outer shell (typically 4-7), so:
- It's difficult to lose them all to form positive ions
- It's easier to share electrons with other non-metals
- Sharing allows both atoms to achieve full outer shells

### Formation of a Covalent Bond

**Example: Hydrogen (H₂)**

- Each H atom has 1 electron, needs 2 for full shell
- Two H atoms share their electrons
- Both atoms now have 2 electrons in their outer shell

[DOT-CROSS: H₂ molecule showing shared pair of electrons]

$$\text{H} \cdot + \cdot \text{H} \rightarrow \text{H-H}$$

### Types of Covalent Bonds

| Bond Type | Electrons Shared | Symbol | Example |
|-----------|------------------|--------|--------|
| Single bond | 2 (one pair) | — | H-H, C-C |
| Double bond | 4 (two pairs) | = | O=O, C=C |
| Triple bond | 6 (three pairs) | ≡ | N≡N, C≡C |

More electrons shared = stronger bond

### Drawing Dot-and-Cross Diagrams

**Rules:**
1. Show only outer shell electrons
2. Use dots for one atom, crosses for another
3. Shared pairs go between the atoms
4. Each atom should end up with a full outer shell

### Common Covalent Molecules

**1. Hydrogen (H₂)**
- Each H needs 1 more electron
- Share 1 pair → Single bond

[DOT-CROSS: H₂ with shared pair]

**2. Water (H₂O)**
- O needs 2 more electrons
- Each H needs 1 more electron
- O shares with 2 H atoms → Two single bonds
- O has 2 lone pairs

[DOT-CROSS: H₂O showing two shared pairs and two lone pairs on oxygen]

**3. Ammonia (NH₃)**
- N needs 3 more electrons
- Each H needs 1 more electron
- N shares with 3 H atoms → Three single bonds
- N has 1 lone pair

[DOT-CROSS: NH₃ showing three shared pairs and one lone pair on nitrogen]

**4. Methane (CH₄)**
- C needs 4 more electrons
- Each H needs 1 more electron
- C shares with 4 H atoms → Four single bonds
- No lone pairs

[DOT-CROSS: CH₄ showing four shared pairs]

**5. Oxygen (O₂)**
- Each O needs 2 more electrons
- Two O atoms share 2 pairs → Double bond
- Each O has 2 lone pairs

[DOT-CROSS: O₂ showing double bond]

**6. Nitrogen (N₂)**
- Each N needs 3 more electrons
- Two N atoms share 3 pairs → Triple bond
- Each N has 1 lone pair

[DOT-CROSS: N₂ showing triple bond]

**7. Carbon Dioxide (CO₂)**
- C needs 4 more electrons
- Each O needs 2 more electrons
- C shares 2 pairs with each O → Two double bonds
- Each O has 2 lone pairs

[DOT-CROSS: CO₂ showing two double bonds]

### Lone Pairs and Bonding Pairs

- **Bonding pair:** A pair of electrons shared between two atoms
- **Lone pair:** A pair of electrons not involved in bonding (belongs to one atom only)

| Molecule | Bonding Pairs | Lone Pairs (on central atom) |
|----------|---------------|------------------------------|
| H₂O | 2 | 2 |
| NH₃ | 3 | 1 |
| CH₄ | 4 | 0 |

### Summary of Common Molecules

| Molecule | Formula | Bonds | Shape |
|----------|---------|-------|-------|
| Hydrogen | H₂ | Single | Linear |
| Chlorine | Cl₂ | Single | Linear |
| Water | H₂O | 2 single | Bent |
| Ammonia | NH₃ | 3 single | Pyramidal |
| Methane | CH₄ | 4 single | Tetrahedral |
| Oxygen | O₂ | Double | Linear |
| Nitrogen | N₂ | Triple | Linear |
| Carbon dioxide | CO₂ | 2 double | Linear |

## Common Mistakes

- **Mistake:** Forgetting to include lone pairs in dot-and-cross diagrams
- **Correct:** Always show all outer shell electrons, including lone pairs

- **Mistake:** Thinking covalent bonds involve electron transfer
- **Correct:** Covalent bonds involve electron sharing

- **Mistake:** Drawing more than 8 electrons around second-row elements
- **Correct:** Most elements (C, N, O, F) can only have 8 electrons in their outer shell

## Practice Questions

1. Define the term 'covalent bond'. (2 marks)

2. Draw dot-and-cross diagrams for:
   a) Hydrogen chloride, HCl (2 marks)
   b) Ammonia, NH₃ (2 marks)
   c) Carbon dioxide, CO₂ (3 marks)

3. Explain why nitrogen gas (N₂) has a triple bond. (3 marks)

4. The molecules H₂O, NH₃, and CH₄ all have different numbers of lone pairs on the central atom. State the number of lone pairs for each. (3 marks)

5. Explain why non-metals form covalent bonds rather than ionic bonds when bonding with other non-metals. (3 marks)

## Key Terms Glossary

| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Covalent bond | A shared pair of electrons between two atoms |
| Single bond | One shared pair of electrons |
| Double bond | Two shared pairs of electrons |
| Triple bond | Three shared pairs of electrons |
| Bonding pair | A pair of electrons shared between two atoms |
| Lone pair | A pair of electrons on one atom, not involved in bonding |

## Summary

- Covalent bonds form when non-metal atoms share electrons
- Shared electrons are attracted to both nuclei, holding atoms together
- Single bonds share 2 electrons; double bonds share 4; triple bonds share 6
- Dot-and-cross diagrams show shared pairs and lone pairs
- Each atom achieves a full outer shell through sharing
- Common molecules: H₂, H₂O, NH₃, CH₄, O₂, N₂, CO₂
